The scent of ivy and old stone was strong on the air.

A shadow passed across the self-same window; the distinct silhouette of a man's head and shoulders, visible for a brief second against the faint, residual light of the sky. He seemed to be standing, looking out, before he stepped back into the blackness of the room.

The quiet evening, which had begun with a vision of titans and a discussion of pride, had ended with a tangible, human mystery. A shadow in a window had eclipsed the grander spectacles of nature and theology, replacing them with a question that was sharp, immediate, and personal. Who was in the Dower House? And for both Frances and Eleanor, the world had suddenly become a far more interesting place.

He spoke the words low, not to the ladies, but to the turf at his feet; yet there was in his tone no bitterness, only a quiet statement of fact. He looked up, and a slow, grave smile touched the corners of his mouth. "A man must have summat, Miss Eleanor, that he calls his own. If it is not land nor gold, it must be his own two hands and the will to use 'em. To ask for help when the strength is in you to help yourself; that is to make yourself a pauper in spirit, and that is a state I cannot abide."

"And you are right, Ames," said Frances, with her characteristic decision. "The pride that keeps a man on his own feet is a virtue; it is the brother of self-respect. It is not the same pride Mr. Armitage commends from the pulpit; the pride of station, the pride of being a gentleman that has never soiled his hands, the pride that looks down on an honest workman as a being of a lower order."

"Ay, that's it, Miss Thorne," said Ames, his face clearing entirely. "You've put the word to it. It is one thing to be proud of your work; it is another to be proud of your idleness. One is the sweat of your brow, the other is the sweat of another man's brow, which you take and call your own."

He seemed about to say more, to elaborate on this distinction which he felt so keenly, but a new figure emerging from the church porch arrested his speech. It was the very man of whom they spoke; Mr. Armitage himself. He was a tall, slender young man, with a pale complexion and hair of a flaxen fairness which he took great pains to arrange. His features were regular, but wanted expression; his eye, a cold, light blue, had a trick of looking over people's heads, as if fixed on some distant spiritual matter, though some said it was merely looking for a better reflection of himself in the window-panes. He advanced towards the little group with a step that was meant to be dignified, but which seemed merely stiff.

"Miss Thorne, Miss Gascoyne," he began, his voice possessing a certain reedy quality, as if strained through layers of propriety. "I was surprised not to see you in your pew this evening. I trust neither of you is unwell?"

"We are perfectly well, thank you, Mr. Armitage," replied Frances, her tone civil but cool. "We found the evening air more to our liking than the air within."

"Ah, nature," said the curate, with a small, indulgent smile, as if speaking of a child's toy. "A fine thing in its place, no doubt. A testament to the Creator's power. But our duty, Miss Thorne, our first duty, is to the sanctuary, to the word. The soul requires its nourishment just as the body does." He let his gaze drift for a moment to Ames, who had become rigid and was staring intently at the distant outline of the moors. The curate's look was not one of recognition, but of classification; he saw not Ames the carpenter, but 'a labouring man.'

"The soul," said Frances, her voice very clear and quiet, "may sometimes find its nourishment where it will. Did not the Psalmist lift up his eyes unto the hills? He did not, I believe, specify that they must be viewed through a church window."

A faint colour rose in Mr. Armitage's pale cheeks. "That is a poetical expression, Miss Thorne. We must not take such things too literally. The church is the appointed place. To neglect it is to set a poor example for--for others." He made a slight, indefinite gesture in Ames's direction.

Eleanor, who had remained silent, now spoke, her voice gentle as always. "Mr. Ames has been in church, Mr. Armitage. He has but now come out with his children."

The curate looked surprised, and for the first time bestowed a direct, if fleeting, glance upon the workman. "Ah. Indeed. That is commendable. Commendable. A man in your station has many temptations to neglect his spiritual duties. I am glad to see you resist them."

Ames said nothing. His face, set as stone, was a mask of impassive resentment. He had touched his cap when the curate approached, a simple mark of respect for the cloth, but he would not be drawn into conversation. He felt the impertinence of the man's praise as a greater insult than any rebuke.

Frances, however, was not inclined to let the speech pass. "Temptations, Mr. Armitage? A man who works twelve hours a day to feed his family has little time for the temptations you perhaps imagine. His chief temptation, I should think, is to despair when he cannot find work, or to bitterness when he is treated with condescension by those who have never wanted for a meal."

The curate was now visibly discomfited. He was not accustomed to being contradicted, least of all by a lady of Miss Thorne's standing, and on such a topic. "My dear Miss Thorne, you are severe. I speak only of the general state of the lower orders. They require guidance, a firm hand."

"They require justice, sir," retorted Frances, "and a little human charity, which is a different thing from clerical patronage. You speak of setting an example. What example is set by a shepherd who does not know his own sheep, who sees his flock only as a nameless mass to be lectured at from a height?"

"I--I perform my duties to the best of my ability," stammered Mr. Armitage, his composure quite shattered. He looked from Frances's flashing eyes to Eleanor's grave, pitying face, and found no comfort in either. He was out of his depth. This was not the polite, vapid drawing-room chat in which he excelled. This was real, and it was disconcerting.

"I am sure you believe so," said Frances, with a finality that was like the closing of a door. There was a moment of exceedingly awkward silence. Mr. Armitage adjusted his cravat.

"Well," he said at last, attempting to recover some shred of his dignity. "The air grows chill. I must not keep you. Miss Gascoyne, your uncle the rector will be wondering at your absence. Good evening to you, ladies." He gave a stiff little bow, which pointedly excluded the third member of their party, and walked away towards the rectory, his back radiating indignation.

When he was out of earshot, Ames drew a long breath, and the rigidity went out of his posture. He passed a hand over his rough hair. "Thank you, Miss Thorne," he said, with a surprising depth of feeling. "Thank you."

"He is a fool, Ames," said Frances brusquely, though her colour was still high. "Pay him no mind."

"It is not easy to pay no mind to a man who thinks you have no mind to pay," replied the carpenter, with a flash of the dry wit that the ladies found so agreeable. He then stooped, gathered a stray tool that had fallen from his bag, and made his own preparations to depart. "The light is going. Jane will be looking for me. Good-night to you, Miss Thorne, Miss Eleanor. And thank you again."

He gave them a nod, a gesture of sincere respect between equals, and set off down the path, his heavy work-boots making a steady, solid sound on the gravel. The two ladies watched him go, a sturdy, independent figure dwindling into the twilight.

"There goes a better Christian than Mr. Armitage will ever be," said Frances, "though he may never read a commentary or puzzle his head over the thirty-nine articles."

"He has a good heart, and a proud one," said Eleanor. "I felt for him, standing there while Mr. Armitage talked over him as if he were a piece of furniture."

"I did not feel for him; I felt with him," said Frances. "My blood boiled. The sheer, unthinking arrogance of that young man! To speak of Ames's 'station' and his 'temptations!' I should like to see Mr. Armitage attempt one day of Ames's work. His temptations would be to lie down in a ditch and weep for his mother."

Eleanor smiled faintly at the image. "You were very formidable, Frances. You routed him completely."

"One must, at times," Frances answered, taking Eleanor's arm as they began to walk slowly away from the churchyard, towards the path that led to the Hall. "Such pride as his must be lanced, or it poisons everything around it. It is the pride of the Pharisee, who thanks God he is not as other men. Ames's pride is that of the freeman, who will not be treated as a slave. The one is an offence to God and man; the other is a man's right."

They walked on in silence for a time. The last fires of the sunset had burned out in the west, leaving a sky of pearl and violet, against which the dark line of the moors was sharply etched. The air was calm and sweet, full of the scent of damp earth and late-blooming roses from the rectory garden. The world seemed to be holding its breath, lapsing into the deep peace of night.

Eleanor's thoughts, which had been stirred by the encounter, began to settle, but not upon the curate or the carpenter. Frances's sharp defence of a man's right to his own soul, her vision of a world ordered by justice rather than station, recalled to Eleanor's mind the earlier, grander vision of her friend Shirley, who had spoken of a woman-Titan, of Mother Eve, of a power vast and elemental. Eleanor did not see titans in the landscape; her imagination was of a quieter, more domestic cast. Yet she, too, felt a longing for something beyond the narrow confines of her daily life; a life comfortable, privileged, yet in some profound sense, incomplete.

Her own thoughts, like Caroline's in the other churchyard, turned to the word "mother," but for Eleanor it was not a person she lacked. Her mother was a gentle, faded presence in a London drawing-room, from whom she received dutiful, affectionate letters filled with news of people she barely knew. No; her longing was for a place, a home that was truly her own. A home she had once been promised, and which now stood empty, a silent reproach on the edge of the estate.

As they cleared the trees that fringed the churchyard, the house came into view. It was the Dower House, a handsome stone building of a much older date than the Hall, with mullioned windows and a steep, gabled roof. It had been unoccupied for years, ever since the death of the Squire's great-aunt, and a faint air of melancholy and neglect hung about it, for all that the grounds were kept tidy. It was to this house that Eleanor's girlish dreams had been pinned; it had been half-promised to her by the old Squire, her guardian, as a future home, should she choose to remain unmarried. The new Squire, his son, had never repeated the promise, and Eleanor had been too proud to ask.

Tonight, as she looked towards it, she gave a sudden start, and her hand tightened on Frances's arm.

"Frances," she whispered. "Look."

Frances followed her gaze. "What is it? I see nothing."

"The window," Eleanor said, her voice hushed. "The upper window on the left. I saw a light."

"A light? Nonsense, Eleanor. It must be a reflection of the moon. It is rising now, behind us."

"No, it was not the moon. It was a warm light, a candle or a lamp. It was there, and then it was gone."

They both stood still on the path, straining their eyes through the gathering dusk. The Dower House stood dark and silent, its windows like vacant eyes. There was no sign of life.

"You imagined it," said Frances, though with less certainty than before. "The house is empty. Who would be in it?"

"I do not know. But I saw it. I am sure I saw it."

A shiver, not entirely from the evening's chill, passed through Eleanor. The house had always held a potent charm for her imagination. She had furnished it a hundred times in her mind, pictured herself sitting in the deep embrasure of that very window, reading by the firelight, the mistress of her own small domain. The thought that a stranger might be there, a squatter perhaps, or someone let in by secret arrangement, struck her with a strange, personal sense of violation.

"Let us walk a little closer," Frances suggested, her own curiosity now piqued. "If there is a poacher or a vagrant sheltering there, the Squire should be told."

They left the main path and struck across the damp grass of the park, their light dresses brushing against the overgrown clumps of clover and thyme. The silence was profound, broken only by the soft crush of their own footsteps and the distant, mournful cry of a peewit. As they drew nearer to the house, its dark mass loomed larger, more imposing. The scent of ivy and old stone was strong on the air.

They stopped by a low stone wall that separated the lawns from the house's immediate garden. All was still. The window Eleanor had indicated remained stubbornly dark.

"You must have been mistaken, my dear," Frances said softly. "There is no one."

But even as she spoke, they both saw it. Not a light this time, but a movement. A shadow passed across the self-same window; the distinct silhouette of a man's head and shoulders, visible for a brief second against the faint, residual light of the sky. He seemed to be standing, looking out, before he stepped back into the blackness of the room.

The two women looked at each other, their eyes wide. It was no illusion. There was someone in the empty house.

"Who can it be?" Eleanor breathed, her heart beating fast. "No one has a key but the Squire and Mr. Moore, the bailiff."

"Moore would have no reason to be there at this hour," Frances mused. "And the Squire is in London. It is very strange. A secret, Eleanor. We have stumbled upon a secret."

Frances's eyes gleamed with the love of a mystery. She was, at heart, a strategist, a general; a puzzle, a hidden campaign, was a tonic to her spirit. Eleanor felt a different emotion; a tremor of fear, but also of a strange, inexplicable hope. The empty house was no longer empty. Life, of a secret and unknown kind, had returned to it. The dream she had cherished was disturbed, but it was also, in a way, made more real. The house was alive again.

They stood for a long moment, watching, but nothing further stirred. The house kept its secret. At last, Frances drew her friend away.

"Come," she said, her voice low and excited. "We can do no more tonight. But we will solve this, Eleanor. We will discover who our mysterious neighbour is. Tomorrow, we shall begin our inquiries."

They walked back towards the great, lighted bulk of the Hall, their minds whirling with speculation. The quiet evening, which had begun with a vision of titans and a discussion of pride, had ended with a tangible, human mystery. A shadow in a window had eclipsed the grander spectacles of nature and theology, replacing them with a question that was sharp, immediate, and personal. Who was in the Dower House? And why was he there in secret, like a thief in the night? The peace of the countryside had been broken, not by the tramp of soldiers, but by the quiet flicker of a single, illicit candle. And for both Frances and Eleanor, the world had suddenly become a far more interesting place.

It had been bent just enough to allow a slender person to squeeze through the gap, and then bent back to look, from a distance, as if it were still in place. The stone around it was scraped, and a few fresh flecks of rust lay on the sill.

The moon was rising, a sliver of silver that cast long, distorted shadows and made the familiar landscape seem strange and new. They found a place of concealment in the same rhododendron thicket they had used that afternoon, a natural arbour that gave them a clear view of the back of the Dower House.

The minutes turned into an hour. The world was utterly silent, save for the occasional hoot of an owl or the rustle of some small creature in the undergrowth. The Dower House stood like a tomb, dark and lifeless. Caroline began to shiver, and not entirely from cold. The whole enterprise now seemed mad, a girlish folly.

"He will not come," she whispered. "We were wrong."

"Hush," Shirley commanded, her hand closing on Caroline's wrist. "Listen."

Caroline strained her ears. At first, she heard nothing. Then, she caught it: a faint, rhythmic sound, regular and low. It was the sound of a saw. Someone was sawing wood, not with the rough tear of a large saw, but with the finer, more careful stroke of a small one. The sound came from within the house.

Their mysterious resident was not only present; he was at work.

They watched, their breath held. The sawing stopped. A long period of silence followed. Then, what they had been waiting for: a light appeared. It was in the same upper-left window as the night before. But this time, it was not a brief flicker. A candle was lit, and it remained, casting a steady, soft yellow square upon the darkness. It was not shielded. The occupant, believing himself secure in the depths of the night, had grown confident.

And then, he appeared. A figure passed in front of the window, his silhouette thrown into sharp relief. It was the same man's form they had seen before, but now they saw him more clearly. He was tall, and seemed to have a bearing of some refinement, even in shadow. He was not looking out, but seemed to be moving about the room. He stopped, and his shadow-form bent over what must have been a table. His hands were busy with some delicate task, his head bowed in concentration.

He was not a thief ransacking the place, nor a vagrant making a rough camp. He was a man engaged in some quiet, settled occupation, as if he were in his own study.

"Who is he?" Caroline breathed, her mind racing through impossibilities. "A political fugitive? A debtor in hiding? An artist?"

"I do not know," Shirley said, her voice tight with excitement. "But I mean to find out." She looked at Caroline, her face pale and determined in the moonlight. "Are you brave, Caroline?"

"I do not think so," Caroline answered honestly.

"You are braver than you know. Tomorrow, we move to the final phase. We will contrive to speak to him."

"Speak to him? How? By shouting through the window?"

"No. I have a better idea. A letter. We shall write a letter, and leave it for him where he will find it. We will leave it by his secret door."

The audacity of the plan took Caroline's breath away. To communicate with the shadow, to invite a response, to turn their spying into an exchange. It was a step into the unknown, a direct challenge to the mystery. It was, in short, pure Shirley Keeldar. And as fear warred with fascination in Caroline's heart, she knew, with a strange certainty, that she would agree. The lure of the secret was now too strong to resist. The man in the Dower House was no longer a mere object of curiosity; he was becoming a character in the story of their lives.

"A man must have summat to hold on to. When work was gone, and the belly was empty, and bigger men than me were taking parish bread, I said to my wife, 'We'll not do it. We'll sell the clock first.' And we did. But we kept our own roof and our own name clean. That's a kind of pride, I suppose."

"It is the best kind, William," said Shirley, her tone losing its ironic edge and becoming earnest and warm. "It is the pride of a free man, who knows his own worth, though it be not measured in guineas. That is a Titan's pride, is it not? The sort that would rather be chained to a rock than bow to a tyrant."

William looked up, a little perplexed by the reference, but he caught the spirit of her praise. A slow, gratified smile spread over his face. "Well, miss, I never thought of it in that light. But I thank you."

"And your wife, Mary, she agreed with you?" Caroline asked, her thoughts still on that theme of fortitude.

"She did, miss. Mary's got a spirit of her own. She'd sooner live on water and a crust of her own baking than be beholden to any." He bounced the little boy, Martin, on his knee. "This little lad, he's the reason for it all. For him and for these two," he added, nodding towards his daughters who sat listening with grave attention. "We want them to grow up and not be ashamed of their father and mother."

A silence fell, a comfortable one, filled with the sounds of the summer evening: the hum of a beetle, the last notes of a blackbird, the faint, far-off strains of the organ from the church. The scene was one of perfect rustic peace; the rough-hewn working man, his children neat and clean about him, framed against the ancient grey stones of the churchyard, with the two graceful ladies standing before him. It was a picture of England, of its settled orders and its deep, quiet heart. Yet under the surface, all was in motion: Caroline's soul was a sea of filial longing; Shirley's mind was peopled with visions of mythical power and earthly glory; and William Farren's heart harboured a sturdy, resentful independence that was a sign of the changing times. Even the soldiers, whose passing had briefly disturbed them, were a symptom of a deeper unrest, of troubles brewing in the nearby valleys, of looms being broken and mills threatened.

"The sermon will be over soon," Caroline said at last, her sense of propriety stirring. "Perhaps we should not be seen loitering."

"Let them see us," Shirley replied with a careless air. "Let them say, 'Miss Keeldar prefers the society of William Farren to that of Mr. Donne.' They would be right. I do. There is more truth in William's little finger than in that curate's whole body."

William shuffled his feet, embarrassed but pleased. "Nay, Miss Shirley, ye shouldn't say so."

"But I should, and I will. Good-night, William. Give my regards to Mary, and tell her that if she has any more of those currant buns, I will call for one tomorrow." She smiled, a flash of brilliance that lit her whole face, and with a nod, she turned. Caroline offered her own gentle good-night, with a soft pat for the little girls' heads, and followed her friend.

They did not take the path towards the rectory gate, but instead, by a common unspoken impulse, they walked back towards the brow of the hill, where they had stood before. The west was now a deep, smouldering claret, and the first stars were sharp and silver in the immense vault of the sky. The air had grown cooler, carrying the scent of dew on the grass.

"A good man, that Farren," Shirley said, breaking the silence. "Stubborn as a Yorkshire rock, but as sound."

"His pride is not like the pride you spoke of earlier, Shirley. Not the curates' pride of office."

"No," Shirley agreed. "Theirs is a hollow gourd; his is a solid oak. Theirs is fastened to a title, a position; his is rooted in himself. He could be stripped of everything he owns, and he would still be William Farren, a man who will not bend his neck. They, if they were unfrocked and unnamed, what would they be? Nothing. Mere shorn sheep."

They walked on, their dresses whispering against the overgrown clumps of clover and thyme. The silence was profound, broken only by the soft crush of their own footsteps and the distant, mournful cry of a peewit. As they drew nearer to Fieldhead, Shirley's home, its dark mass loomed larger, more imposing. The scent of ivy and old stone was strong on the air. They stopped by a low stone wall that separated the lawns from a smaller, more isolated dwelling that stood in its own overgrown garden some distance from the main house. This was the Dower House, long unoccupied.

All was still. The windows were black, vacant eyes in the stone face of the building. "It looks a lonely place," Caroline said softly. "I wonder no one has lived there for so long."

"The last dowager did not like it; she preferred Bath," Shirley answered, her gaze fixed on the house. "And since her death, it has been waiting. For what, I do not know. A new mistress, perhaps." She paused, then touched Caroline's arm, her voice dropping to a whisper. "Look. At the upper window. The one on the left."

Caroline's eyes followed her friend's pointing finger. At first, she saw nothing but the dark pane reflecting the dying sky. But then, she saw it. Not a light, but a flicker within the darkness. A faint, transient spark, as if a candle had been lit and then instantly extinguished or shielded. It was there for a second, and then gone.

"Did you see?" Shirley breathed.

"Yes. A light. But it might have been a reflection, Shirley. A star."

"No star flickers so low on the horizon, and with such a yellow cast. It was a candle, Caroline. There is someone in the Dower House."

A thrill, half of fear, half of excitement, ran through Caroline. The house was meant to be empty, locked, its keys in the keeping of Mr. Yorke, the steward, miles away. "Who can it be? A vagrant?"

"A vagrant would not be so careful to hide his light. He would not trouble himself with the upper floors. He would break into the kitchens and sleep by the cold hearth. No. This is something else." Shirley's eyes gleamed in the twilight with the love of a mystery. She was, at heart, a general; a puzzle, a hidden campaign, was a tonic to her spirit. "We have stumbled upon a secret."

They stood for a long moment, watching, but nothing further stirred. The house kept its secret, wrapped in the gathering darkness and its own mantle of ivy. The absolute stillness was more unnerving than the flicker of light had been. It was the silence of a held breath.

"Come," Caroline said at last, pulling at Shirley's sleeve. "It is late, and it is not our affair."

"Not our affair?" Shirley echoed, her voice alive with suppressed energy. "A strange man lodging secretly in my house, on my land, and it is not my affair? Caroline, you have no sense of property! It is entirely my affair. It is a trespass, a riddle, a romance! We will solve it."

"How can we? We cannot go and knock on the door."

"No, not tonight. That would be to show our hand. We must be cunning. We shall begin our inquiries tomorrow. We will be detectives, you and I."

They walked back towards the great, lighted bulk of Fieldhead, their minds whirling with speculation. The quiet evening, which had begun with a vision of titans and a discussion of pride, had ended with a tangible, human mystery. A spark in a window had eclipsed the grander spectacles of nature and theology, replacing them with a question that was sharp, immediate, and personal. Who was in the Dower House? And why was he there in secret, like a thief in the night?

The next morning rose bright and clear, painting the world in honest daylight. From her window, Caroline could see the Dower House, looking solid, respectable, and utterly inanimate. Its grey stones were warmed by the sun; a few martins dipped and soared about its chimneys. It was impossible to believe it held a secret. It seemed to Caroline that the flicker of light, the whispered conjectures, must all have been a dream born of the twilight and Shirley's vivid imagination.

She found her friend in the breakfast-parlour, not sharing her doubts. Shirley was already dressed for the outdoors, a list written on a slip of paper before her, an air of brisk command about her.

"Good morning, Caroline," she said, looking up from her list. "I have been forming a plan of campaign. First, we must discover if there is any legitimate reason for a person to be in the house. A survey, repairs, anything of that nature."

"And how are we to do that without raising suspicion?"

"Easily. I shall send for the steward's books. I have a right to see them. I shall profess a sudden interest in the cost of maintaining the outlying properties. While I am engaged in that dry task, you, Caroline, will pursue a different line of inquiry."

"I?" Caroline asked, a little alarmed.

"Yes, you. You have a softer touch than I. You will go and visit Mrs. Gill, the housekeeper here at Fieldhead. You will talk of jams and linens, and then you will artfully turn the conversation to the Dower House. Has she heard any sounds? Has young Robert, the garden-lad, seen anyone near there? Servants' gossip is a mighty river, Caroline; we must fish in it."

Caroline agreed, though she felt ill-suited to the part of a spy. Her interview with Mrs. Gill proved fruitless. The housekeeper was a stout, literal woman, whose mind did not run to mysteries. She had heard nothing and seen nothing, and was more interested in a moth that had got into the winter blankets.

Shirley, meanwhile, had spent an hour with Mr. Yorke's leather-bound ledgers. She found expenditures for mending the Dower House roof the previous autumn, and a note about clearing the gutters, but nothing more recent. No mention of any ongoing work, no permission granted for anyone to enter.

"So," Shirley declared, closing the last ledger with a decisive snap. "The man is there without authority. He is an interloper. Phase one of the investigation is complete. Now for phase two."

"Which is?"

"We must reconnoitre the ground ourselves. In broad daylight."

They put on their hats and walking-boots and set out. To any observer, they were merely two young ladies taking a constitutional walk about the grounds. But their steps were bent with purpose towards the silent house. They did not approach it directly, but made a wide circle, coming up behind it where a thicket of overgrown rhododendrons offered cover.

The back of the house was less prepossessing than the front. A small, flagged courtyard was green with moss, and a pump stood rusting by the scullery door. Everything was still, asleep in the midday sun. The windows were dirty, webbed with spiders' labours.

"There is no sign of life," Caroline whispered, feeling rather foolish.

"Patience," Shirley breathed, her eyes scanning every detail. "An intruder would be careful. He would not leave his boots on the step. Look there."

She pointed. By the scullery door, half hidden by a clump of docks, was a single, fresh footprint in a patch of damp earth. It was large, the mark of a man's boot, and clearly recent; the edges were still sharp. More than that, propped carefully against the wall nearby, was a small stack of wood, neatly sawn and split. It was not old, rotted wood from the grounds; it looked like seasoned ash, brought from elsewhere.

"He is not a mere vagrant," Shirley murmured, her brow furrowed in thought. "A vagrant would burn green wood, anything he could break. This man makes provision. He intends to stay. And he is tidy."

"But how does he get in and out, Shirley? The doors are locked. We saw that."

"The windows, perhaps. Let us examine them."

They crept along the wall, peering at each of the ground-floor windows. They were all shut fast, clouded with the grime of years. Then, at the very end, they found it. The pantry window. It was small, and barred, but one of the bars had been worked loose from the stone at its lower end. It had been bent just enough to allow a slender person to squeeze through the gap, and then bent back to look, from a distance, as if it were still in place. The stone around it was scraped, and a few fresh flecks of rust lay on the sill.

"This is his door," Shirley said in triumph. "He comes and goes by night, like a fox. He is clever. But we are cleverer." She stood back, her mind working. "He has firewood. That means he has a fire. But a fire makes smoke. We have seen no smoke from the chimneys."

"Perhaps he only lights it at night," Caroline suggested. "And uses dry wood that smokes little."

"Perhaps. Or perhaps he uses a chimney that is not easily seen. The one at the back, behind the main stack. Yes. It is all of a piece. He is cautious, methodical, and strong enough to bend iron." A strange expression crossed Shirley's face; a look of admiration, almost. "I confess, my trespasser begins to interest me. He is no common thief."

"What shall we do, Shirley? Tell Mr. Yorke?"

"And have him send two clumsy constables to frighten him away or arrest him? To have the whole neighbourhood chattering about it? No. That would be a crude and unsatisfactory conclusion. It would be like shooting a rare bird instead of studying its habits. We will watch. We will wait. Tonight, Caroline, we will keep a vigil."

Caroline's heart sank a little at the prospect. A night-time vigil sounded cold and frightening. Yet she could not deny the pull of the mystery, a fascination that was fast overriding her fear. There was a story in that house, and she felt a desperate, inexplicable need to know the ending; or perhaps, the beginning.

That evening, after the household was abed, the two friends slipped out of a side door of Fieldhead, cloaked against the night's chill. The moon was rising, a sliver of silver that cast long, distorted shadows and made the familiar landscape seem strange and new. They found a place of concealment in the same rhododendron thicket they had used that afternoon, a natural arbour that gave them a clear view of the back of the Dower House.

The minutes turned into an hour. The world was utterly silent, save for the occasional hoot of an owl or the rustle of some small creature in the undergrowth. The Dower House stood like a tomb, dark and lifeless. Caroline began to shiver, and not entirely from cold. The whole enterprise now seemed mad, a girlish folly.

"He will not come," she whispered. "We were wrong."

"Hush," Shirley commanded, her hand closing on Caroline's wrist. "Listen."

Caroline strained her ears. At first, she heard nothing. Then, she caught it: a faint, rhythmic sound, regular and low. It was the sound of a saw. Someone was sawing wood, not with the rough tear of a large saw, but with the finer, more careful stroke of a small one. The sound came from within the house.

Their mysterious resident was not only present; he was at work.

They watched, their breath held. The sawing stopped. A long period of silence followed. Then, what they had been waiting for: a light appeared. It was in the same upper-left window as the night before. But this time, it was not a brief flicker. A candle was lit, and it remained, casting a steady, soft yellow square upon the darkness. It was not shielded. The occupant, believing himself secure in the depths of the night, had grown confident.

And then, he appeared. A figure passed in front of the window, his silhouette thrown into sharp relief. It was the same man's form they had seen before, but now they saw him more clearly. He was tall, and seemed to have a bearing of some refinement, even in shadow. He was not looking out, but seemed to be moving about the room. He stopped, and his shadow-form bent over what must have been a table. His hands were busy with some delicate task, his head bowed in concentration.

He was not a thief ransacking the place, nor a vagrant making a rough camp. He was a man engaged in some quiet, settled occupation, as if he were in his own study.

"Who is he?" Caroline breathed, her mind racing through impossibilities. "A political fugitive? A debtor in hiding? An artist?"

"I do not know," Shirley said, her voice tight with excitement. "But I mean to find out." She looked at Caroline, her face pale and determined in the moonlight. "Are you brave, Caroline?"

"I do not think so," Caroline answered honestly.

"You are braver than you know. Tomorrow, we move to the final phase. We will contrive to speak to him."

"Speak to him? How? By shouting through the window?"

"No. I have a better idea. A letter. We shall write a letter, and leave it for him where he will find it. We will leave it by his secret door."

The audacity of the plan took Caroline's breath away. To communicate with the shadow, to invite a response, to turn their spying into an exchange. It was a step into the unknown, a direct challenge to the mystery. It was, in short, pure Shirley Keeldar. And as fear warred with fascination in Caroline's heart, she knew, with a strange certainty, that she would agree. The lure of the secret was now too strong to resist. The man in the Dower House was no longer a mere object of curiosity; he was becoming a character in the story of their lives.

"A man has his pride, Miss Caroline," he said, his voice low and a little stubborn. "It is all some of us have to keep our coats on our backs. To go begging is to say another man is your master in all things; to take credit is to sell your tomorrow for a crust today. My children will not learn that lesson from me. Shirley nodded, her keen eyes approving the sentiment. "It is the pride of a Titan, William, who would rather be chained to a rock than bow to a tyrant. You have more of the old blood in you than all the curates in Christendom."

First came the humble folk, fanning out towards the village paths; then the more substantial tenant-farmers and shopkeepers, who paused to exchange sober greetings.
And then came the very men of whom they had been speaking. Mr. Donne, tall and slim, was adjusting the hang of his surplice with a delicate, almost feline, touch; he had an air of believing the very light of day was arranged for his particular benefit. Beside him, a stark contrast, strode the Reverend Peter Malone, a great, florid man with a voice accustomed to filling chapels and silencing dissent. He carried his large frame with an assertive roll, as if the churchyard itself were a territory he had personally conquered. Bringing up the rear, like a small boat in the wake of two galleons, was little Mr. Sweeting, his pleasant, rosy face full of a mild anxiety to please everyone and offend no one.
"Miss Keeldar!" boomed Mr. Malone, his eyes lighting upon Shirley with a look of proprietary challenge. "Playing the heathen out here with your nature-worship, are we? I trust the sermon you found in these stones was an orthodox one."
Shirley met his gaze without a flicker of deference. Her lips curved in a smile that was all polite amusement and no warmth. "Mr. Malone, I find my sermons in stones and my God in everything; a broader parish than yours, I fancy, and with a more constant congregation. As for orthodoxy, I leave that to those who require such fences to keep their faith from straying."
Mr. Donne gave a little, silvery laugh, a sound as affected as the positioning of his hands. "Now, now, Malone. Miss Keeldar is ever poetical. One must not take her flights of fancy for theological error. A lovely evening, is it not, Miss Helstone?" He turned his attention to Caroline, his condescension softening into what he imagined was a charming grace. "The air is quite bucolic. A pleasant change from the stuffiness of the church."

"Bucolic perhaps," grumbled Malone, not to be so easily deflected, "but the proper place for a Christian gentlewoman on a Sunday evening is within the house of God, not conversing with gardeners in the graveyard. Duty, Miss Keeldar, duty before pleasure."
"You mistake the matter entirely, sir," Shirley replied, her voice acquiring a dangerously sweet edge. "My conversation with Mr. Farren here has been a lesson in duty; a duty to one's children, and a duty to one's own soul. It is a finer lesson than many I have heard preached from a pulpit. Is it not, William?"
William, thus appealed to, shifted his weight and cleared his throat. He looked at Mr. Malone as if he were a piece of rotten timber. "A man does what he must, sir," he said. "And a man knows who speaks sense and who speaks wind."
Malone's florid face darkened to purple. He was not accustomed to such plain speaking from the lower orders. He swelled, preparing some crushing retort, but at that moment a figure appeared in the church porch who commanded more authority than any of them. It was Mr. Helstone.

The sight of her uncle sent a familiar chill through Caroline’s veins. He was to her not a father, but a law; not a comfort, but a command. The tender, impossible vision she had entertained but a moment before, of a mother's loving embrace, dissolved into the harsh reality of her guardian’s presence. He was the embodiment of the life she knew: a life of duties without love, of provision without tenderness, of a home that was a rectory and not a sanctuary. The longing that had surged in her heart now receded, leaving behind a cold ache of resignation. He would call her, and she would come; he would direct, and she would obey. The curates, their petty squabble interrupted, trailed in his wake like a disordered flock. Mr. Malone cast a final, baleful glare at Shirley; Mr. Donne offered a condescending little wave to Caroline; Mr. Sweeting gave a timid, friendly smile to them both, a silent apology for his brethren.

The two little girls, who had been standing silent and grave, models of good behaviour, came to his side. He touched his hat again. "Good-evening to you, Miss Keeldar, Miss Helstone."

"He is always the same," Caroline said, her voice little more than a whisper.

Instead, he is a rock to break oneself against. No matter. We have other things to consider than the tempers of clergymen."
They had reached the gates of Fieldhead. The old hall loomed before them, its many windows dark save for a welcoming light in the parlour. The air was fragrant with the scent of night-stock from the gardens.
"Did you mark Malone's impertinence?" Shirley continued, her mood shifting back to indignation. "To lecture me on my duty! Me! A landowner, a free woman, to be chided by a salaried Irishman with the manners of a drover. If I were a man, I should have called him out."
"What would you have done?" Caroline asked, a faint smile touching her lips despite her own melancholy.
"I should have challenged him to a duel of wits, but he is unarmed. A duel of fists, perhaps, but it would be an unfair contest; his are so much larger than mine. No, the best weapon against such men is the one I used: a contempt so polite they cannot quite grasp it. It puzzles them, and a puzzled bully is a neutralized bully."
They passed through the gate and walked up the gravel drive. The house, Shirley's house, felt like a fortress of feminine independence after the encounters of the evening. Here, she was mistress; here, her will was law.
"Still," Shirley said, as they mounted the steps to the front door, "I confess, their collective foolishness wearies me. The airs they give themselves! One would think that to be ordained was to be remade in a finer clay. Yet as William so wisely noted, the office does nought to magnify the man. It merely places his smallness on a higher pedestal for all to see."
She pushed open the heavy door, and they stepped into the hall. A maid appeared to take their bonnets. The warmth and light of the house enveloped them.
"And yet," Caroline said, finding her voice at last as they moved towards the parlour, "Mr. Sweeting is not like them. He is kind."
"Kind, yes," Shirley conceded, pausing at the parlour door. "He is a good little man, as a lap-dog is a good little dog. He wishes to please. But there is no fire in him, Caroline. No grandeur. He would never strive to scale heaven, nor would he bear a thousand years of bondage. He would simply write a pretty verse about it, and hope it did not offend the bishop. I prefer William’s stubborn pride, or even Robert Moore’s grim battle, to Mr. Sweeting’s harmless insipidity."
She looked at Caroline, her expression softening from its fiery scorn to a look of deep, searching affection. "You are tired. The evening has been too much for you. That longing for your mother... it came back very strongly, did it not?"
Caroline nodded, her eyes filling with tears she had held back in the churchyard. "When I saw William with his children... and then Mr. Helstone... it was... difficult."
"I know." Shirley put her arm around Caroline's shoulders and drew her into the comfortable parlour. A fire was laid in the grate, though unlit on this warm evening, and the room was filled with the scent of dried lavender and old books. "His coldness is a constant reproach to your warm heart. But you must not let it quench you. Your capacity for love is a rare and precious thing, child. Do not let the winter of the rectory freeze the spring in your soul."
She led Caroline to a sofa and sat beside her, taking her hand. "Forget the curates and the rectors for a night. Let us have some tea, and you shall read to me. Let us enter a world of paper and ink, a world of finer feelings and nobler men than any we met in the churchyard today. Excepting William, of course. We will always except William."
And as Caroline leaned her head against her friend's shoulder, feeling the steadfast, loyal strength of her presence, a little of the evening's chill began to dissipate. The harsh figures of Malone and Helstone faded, the painful vision of Robert Moore softened, and the ache in her heart was soothed, if not cured, by the simple, profound comfort of a kindred spirit. The world outside was full of struggle and cold pride, but here, within the walls of Fieldhead, there was for a time, at least, a sanctuary of warmth and understanding.

William’s weather-beaten face, which had been open and pleased, clouded over; a flush of dull red rose under his tanned skin. He looked down at the child on his knee, his rough hand stroking the boy’s ruddy hair.
"A man has his pride, Miss Caroline," he said, his voice low and a little stubborn. "It is all some of us have to keep our coats on our backs. To go begging is to say another man is your master in all things; to take credit is to sell your tomorrow for a crust today. My children will not learn that lesson from me. They will learn that their father’s hands can keep them, or they will learn how to want with a still tongue." He glanced up, not at Caroline, but at Shirley, a sort of challenge in his eye. "There is a pride in that, as you say, miss; but it is not the pride of a fine house, it is the pride of a whole man."
Shirley nodded, her keen eyes approving the sentiment. "It is the pride of a Titan, William, who would rather be chained to a rock than bow to a tyrant. You have more of the old blood in you than all the curates in Christendom."
Before William could reply to this high praise, the great oak doors of the church groaned open, and a sound, not of praise but of shuffling feet and muted coughs, issued forth. The evening service was concluded. A stream of soberly clad parishioners began to emerge, blinking in the lingering daylight, their faces set in expressions of Sunday piety. First came the humble folk, fanning out towards the village paths; then the more substantial tenant-farmers and shopkeepers, who paused to exchange sober greetings.
And then came the very men of whom they had been speaking. Mr. Donne, tall and slim, was adjusting the hang of his surplice with a delicate, almost feline, touch; he had an air of believing the very light of day was arranged for his particular benefit. Beside him, a stark contrast, strode the Reverend Peter Malone, a great, florid man with a voice accustomed to filling chapels and silencing dissent. He carried his large frame with an assertive roll, as if the churchyard itself were a territory he had personally conquered. Bringing up the rear, like a small boat in the wake of two galleons, was little Mr. Sweeting, his pleasant, rosy face full of a mild anxiety to please everyone and offend no one.
"Miss Keeldar!" boomed Mr. Malone, his eyes lighting upon Shirley with a look of proprietary challenge. "Playing the heathen out here with your nature-worship, are we? I trust the sermon you found in these stones was an orthodox one."
Shirley met his gaze without a flicker of deference. Her lips curved in a smile that was all polite amusement and no warmth. "Mr. Malone, I find my sermons in stones and my God in everything; a broader parish than yours, I fancy, and with a more constant congregation. As for orthodoxy, I leave that to those who require such fences to keep their faith from straying."
Mr. Donne gave a little, silvery laugh, a sound as affected as the positioning of his hands. "Now, now, Malone. Miss Keeldar is ever poetical. One must not take her flights of fancy for theological error. A lovely evening, is it not, Miss Helstone?" He turned his attention to Caroline, his condescension softening into what he imagined was a charming grace. "The air is quite bucolic. A pleasant change from the stuffiness of the church."
"It is very fine," Caroline murmured, feeling, as she often did in the presence of these men, a desire to become invisible. She was acutely aware of William Farren beside them, silent and watchful, his peasant’s judgment weighing them all.
"Bucolic perhaps," grumbled Malone, not to be so easily deflected, "but the proper place for a Christian gentlewoman on a Sunday evening is within the house of God, not conversing with gardeners in the graveyard. Duty, Miss Keeldar, duty before pleasure."
"You mistake the matter entirely, sir," Shirley replied, her voice acquiring a dangerously sweet edge. "My conversation with Mr. Farren here has been a lesson in duty; a duty to one's children, and a duty to one's own soul. It is a finer lesson than many I have heard preached from a pulpit. Is it not, William?"
William, thus appealed to, shifted his weight and cleared his throat. He looked at Mr. Malone as if he were a piece of rotten timber. "A man does what he must, sir," he said. "And a man knows who speaks sense and who speaks wind."
Malone's florid face darkened to purple. He was not accustomed to such plain speaking from the lower orders. He swelled, preparing some crushing retort, but at that moment a figure appeared in the church porch who commanded more authority than any of them. It was Mr. Helstone.
The rector stood for a moment, his stern, iron-grey features surveying the scene. His eye took in his niece, Miss Keeldar, the curates, and William Farren with his children. It was a glance that judged and dismissed in a single sweep.
The sight of her uncle sent a familiar chill through Caroline’s veins. He was to her not a father, but a law; not a comfort, but a command. The tender, impossible vision she had entertained but a moment before, of a mother's loving embrace, dissolved into the harsh reality of her guardian’s presence. He was the embodiment of the life she knew: a life of duties without love, of provision without tenderness, of a home that was a rectory and not a sanctuary. The longing that had surged in her heart now receded, leaving behind a cold ache of resignation. He would call her, and she would come; he would direct, and she would obey. That was the whole of their bond.
"Caroline," he said, his voice crisp and devoid of warmth. "It grows late. You and Miss Keeldar will take a chill."
"We are quite warm, thank you, sir," Shirley answered for them both, her tone respectful but not in the least subservient. "We were just admiring the sunset."
Mr. Helstone’s gaze lingered on her, a flicker of something, perhaps reluctant admiration for her spirit, perhaps mere annoyance at her independence, in his eyes. He did not deign to argue. He gave a curt nod that included them all in its dismissal and turned to walk down the path towards the rectory gate. The curates, their petty squabble interrupted, trailed in his wake like a disordered flock. Mr. Malone cast a final, baleful glare at Shirley; Mr. Donne offered a condescending little wave to Caroline; Mr. Sweeting gave a timid, friendly smile to them both, a silent apology for his brethren.
As they disappeared behind the rectory wall, Shirley turned to William. "They are gone, William. The magnificent office has departed, though the men remain as small as ever."
William permitted himself a grim smile. He hoisted his little boy higher on his shoulder. "They're a poor lot, miss. All starch and no substance. Well, we must be on our way. Come, lasses." The two little girls, who had been standing silent and grave, models of good behaviour, came to his side. He touched his hat again. "Good-evening to you, Miss Keeldar, Miss Helstone."
"Good-evening, William," said Caroline, her voice soft. She looked at the sturdy, tender father and his neat, quiet children, and felt a pang of something like envy for their simple, solid affection.
They watched the little family make its way down the path, the children’s steps quickening to keep up with their father’s stride. The churchyard was quiet again, save for the cawing of a distant rook. The deep-burning west, which Shirley had invoked, was now a blaze of orange and violet, streaked with bars of solemn grey cloud.
"And then there was one other," Shirley said quietly, her gaze fixed not on the departing Farrens, but on a point further down the road.
Caroline followed her look. A man stood apart from the last of the dispersing congregation, near the lych-gate, as if he had been a spectator to the entire scene. He had not come from the church; he seemed rather to have just arrived, a solitary figure against the dramatic sky. He stood with his arms crossed over his chest, his head bent, seemingly lost in thought. His posture spoke of cares that had little to do with evening prayers or parish gossip. It was Robert Moore.
A pang, sharp and familiar, went through Caroline’s heart. She had not expected to see him. He so rarely attended service, pleading the pressures of his mill, the endless accounts and correspondence that were his true religion. To see him here, now, at the close of this strange, emotionally charged evening, was an unexpected disturbance. He looked weary, and stern; the lines of his face, even from this distance, seemed etched by anxiety. Was he watching them? No, his gaze was directed towards the ground, or perhaps towards the darkening valley where his mill lay, a place of contention and danger.
He must have felt their eyes upon him, for he looked up suddenly. His glance met theirs, held for a second, and then he gave a brief, almost curt, nod of acknowledgement before turning and walking away, not towards his cottage, but down the lane that led back towards the Hollow.
"He walks like a man with the weight of the world on his shoulders," Shirley observed, her voice thoughtful. "And he chooses to walk towards trouble, not away from it. There is something of your Titan in him too, Caroline, though a darker, more troubled one than William."
Caroline did not answer. Her heart was a confused flutter of feelings. The sight of him, so isolated and burdened, awakened in her a painful tenderness, a desire to offer comfort that she knew she could not give, that he would not accept. He was locked in a world of his own, a world of machines and ledgers and threats of violence, a world into which she, a rector's niece, had no entry.
"Come," said Shirley, gently taking her arm. "My mother Eve grows impatient; the dew is beginning to fall. We must go in."
They walked in silence for a time, leaving the churchyard and taking the path that led up to Fieldhead. The grandeur of the evening was softening into the melancholy of twilight. The vibrant colours were fading from the sky, leaving a placid, luminous green above the blackening silhouettes of the hills.
"A fine collection of men we have in this parish," Shirley remarked at last, breaking the quiet. "A set of proud priests, a prouder workman, and a mill-owner who looks like a tragic hero waiting for the fifth act. What a stage we live upon, Caroline!"
"William is not like the others," Caroline said defensively. "His pride is honest."
"Perfectly honest. It is the pride of self-reliance. The curates' pride is the pride of office, a borrowed garment that fits them ill. Mr. Helstone's is the pride of authority, cold and hard as iron. And Mr. Moore's... his is the pride of a man at war, who will not show a wound for fear it be thought a weakness."
She paused, glancing at her companion's shadowed face. "You are very quiet, dear. Did the sight of your magnificent uncle freeze the words on your tongue?"
"He is always the same," Caroline said, her voice little more than a whisper.
"Yes, he is. As constant as the north star, and as cold. It is a pity. A man with his strength could have been a great comfort, had he a thimbleful of warmth in his constitution. Instead, he is a rock to break oneself against. No matter. We have other things to consider than the tempers of clergymen."
They had reached the gates of Fieldhead. The old hall loomed before them, its many windows dark save for a welcoming light in the parlour. The air was fragrant with the scent of night-stock from the gardens.
"Did you mark Malone's impertinence?" Shirley continued, her mood shifting back to indignation. "To lecture me on my duty! Me! A landowner, a free woman, to be chided by a salaried Irishman with the manners of a drover. If I were a man, I should have called him out."
"What would you have done?" Caroline asked, a faint smile touching her lips despite her own melancholy.
"I should have challenged him to a duel of wits, but he is unarmed. A duel of fists, perhaps, but it would be an unfair contest; his are so much larger than mine. No, the best weapon against such men is the one I used: a contempt so polite they cannot quite grasp it. It puzzles them, and a puzzled bully is a neutralized bully."
They passed through the gate and walked up the gravel drive. The house, Shirley's house, felt like a fortress of feminine independence after the encounters of the evening. Here, she was mistress; here, her will was law.
"Still," Shirley said, as they mounted the steps to the front door, "I confess, their collective foolishness wearies me. The airs they give themselves! One would think that to be ordained was to be remade in a finer clay. Yet as William so wisely noted, the office does nought to magnify the man. It merely places his smallness on a higher pedestal for all to see."
She pushed open the heavy door, and they stepped into the hall. A maid appeared to take their bonnets. The warmth and light of the house enveloped them.
"And yet," Caroline said, finding her voice at last as they moved towards the parlour, "Mr. Sweeting is not like them. He is kind."
"Kind, yes," Shirley conceded, pausing at the parlour door. "He is a good little man, as a lap-dog is a good little dog. He wishes to please. But there is no fire in him, Caroline. No grandeur. He would never strive to scale heaven, nor would he bear a thousand years of bondage. He would simply write a pretty verse about it, and hope it did not offend the bishop. I prefer William’s stubborn pride, or even Robert Moore’s grim battle, to Mr. Sweeting’s harmless insipidity."
She looked at Caroline, her expression softening from its fiery scorn to a look of deep, searching affection. "You are tired. The evening has been too much for you. That longing for your mother... it came back very strongly, did it not?"
Caroline nodded, her eyes filling with tears she had held back in the churchyard. "When I saw William with his children... and then Mr. Helstone... it was... difficult."
"I know." Shirley put her arm around Caroline's shoulders and drew her into the comfortable parlour. A fire was laid in the grate, though unlit on this warm evening, and the room was filled with the scent of dried lavender and old books. "His coldness is a constant reproach to your warm heart. But you must not let it quench you. Your capacity for love is a rare and precious thing, child. Do not let the winter of the rectory freeze the spring in your soul."
She led Caroline to a sofa and sat beside her, taking her hand. "Forget the curates and the rectors for a night. Let us have some tea, and you shall read to me. Let us enter a world of paper and ink, a world of finer feelings and nobler men than any we met in the churchyard today. Excepting William, of course. We will always except William."
And as Caroline leaned her head against her friend's shoulder, feeling the steadfast, loyal strength of her presence, a little of the evening's chill began to dissipate. The harsh figures of Malone and Helstone faded, the painful vision of Robert Moore softened, and the ache in her heart was soothed, if not cured, by the simple, profound comfort of a kindred spirit. The world outside was full of struggle and cold pride, but here, within the walls of Fieldhead, there was for a time, at least, a sanctuary of warmth and understanding.

His gaze lingered on her for a second, a flicker of some unreadable emotion in their depths, before he turned back to Shirley. "Pity, Miss Keeldar?" he said, his voice returning to its former harshness. "Pity is a luxury I cannot afford. Pity does not rebuild a broken frame. Pity does not pay the wages of the honest men who still wish to work. Pity does not stop a bullet. My brother was shot at in his own mill-yard last month. There is your 'grain of justice' for you."
He picked up his hat from the table where he had flung it. "I have said what I came to say. The soldiers are patrolling the Greenclose road. Without another word, he turned and was gone. They heard his heavy, rapid footsteps in the hall, the opening and closing of the great front door, and then the sound of his horse, spurred again into a gallop, fading into the night.
The room he had left felt vast and empty. The air still seemed to vibrate with his restless, angry energy. The spell of the poetry, the peace of the evening, was not merely broken; it was shattered.
Shirley stood for a long moment, staring at the closed door. Then she let out a long breath and sank back into her chair.
"There," she said, her voice laced with a strange, tired admiration. "There goes a man. A hard man, a narrow man, a man of iron and fire, but a man nonetheless. He would not contend with Omnipotence, perhaps, for he does not believe in it. He contends with the next best thing: the world. Did you see his eyes, Caroline, when he spoke of his survival? He is a general in his own private war."
Caroline could not answer. Her throat was tight with unshed tears. The brief moment when he had spoken her name, when his eyes had met hers, had sent a pang of such exquisite pain through her that she could scarcely breathe. He had seen her, and yet he had not seen her. She was a fixture in his life, a cousin, a known quantity, as familiar and as unregarded as the rectory gate or the church spire. The vast, turbulent world of her love for him was a country on a map he never looked at.
"He is very unhappy," she said at last, the words a mere whisper.
Shirley looked at her friend, her own fiery energy softening into a deep, compassionate concern. "Yes," she said gently. "He is very unhappy. And you, my poor bird, have caught his winter's chill. He brings the storm with him wherever he goes, and leaves all in darkness when he departs."
She came and sat on the stool at Caroline's feet, taking her cold hands in her own warm ones. The volume of Scott had fallen to the floor, its pages open to the scene of battle. "He is one of my Titans, you see. A modern Titan, a Prometheus not of fire but of steam, chained to his mill as to a rock, and the vulture that gnaws his vitals is his own ledger-book, his own relentless ambition. And yet, he fights. I cannot help but admire the fight, even as I deplore the cause."
"He thinks we are foolish romantics," Caroline murmured, staring at the fallen book.
"Let him," Shirley retorted, a spark of her old fire returning. "Let him think us fools. He sees the world in black and white, in profit and loss. He does not see the colours of the sunset, nor hear the music in the wind. He does not understand a heart like yours, Caroline. And that, perhaps, is his greatest tragedy of all."
She squeezed Caroline's hands. "Come. The poetry is spoiled for tonight. The world has been too much with us, late and soon. Let us go to bed. Perhaps our dreams will be kinder than our waking hours."
Shirley rose and lit a candle, her own face now looking pale and weary in its gentle glow. The sanctuary had been breached, the peace invaded. As Caroline followed her friend up the grand, silent staircase, she felt the truth of Shirley's words. The harsh figures of the world, embodied so powerfully in Robert Moore, had not faded this time. They had come into the very heart of her refuge, and the ache in her heart, soothed for a brief hour, had returned with a deeper, more desolate pain. The kindred spirit beside her was a comfort, a blessing beyond price; but tonight, the cold pride and the grim struggle of the world felt not only closer, but insurmountable.

His boots were dusty, his face was set in hard, weary lines, and his eyes, dark and intense, swept the room with a rapid, impatient glance. They passed over Caroline as if she were a piece of furniture, a shadow in the corner, and fixed upon Shirley.

He began to pace the length of the Persian rug, his heavy boots scuffing its fine pattern. "I have been riding since it happened, trying to track them. They had help; there are tracks of a cart. They are organized. This is not random anger, Miss Keeldar, this is conspiracy."
"And you have come to tell me this, Mr. Moore? Am I to arm my maidservants and fortify my windows?" Shirley's question had a sharp, ironic edge.
Moore stopped his pacing and turned to face her. "I have come to warn you. You are a landowner, the most significant in this immediate district. Your name carries weight. These men, these frame-breakers, they are stirring up the whole countryside. They speak of tyranny and oppression; they mean the capital and machinery that feed them. They may turn their attention from a tradesman like myself to a person of property like you. Your tenants may be incited. You should be on your guard."
"I thank you for the warning," Shirley said, and there was a dangerous calm in her voice now. "I am on my guard, Mr. Moore. I have been on my guard since the day I came into my inheritance. I see a tragedy in a man who is driven by hunger to destroy the very thing that might, in a better world, have been his salvation."
"A better world!" Moore scoffed, a bitter laugh escaping him. "We do not live in a better world, Miss Keeldar. We live in this one, a world of debt, of risk, of competition. I fight for my survival, and for the survival of the industry this region depends upon. These men, with their nocturnal raids and their brute force, would drag us all back into the dark ages of poverty and famine. Do not romanticize them. They are not your Titans striving against heaven; they are criminals."
He had, unconsciously, thrown her own language back at her. Caroline flinched in her corner, wondering if Shirley would take offence.
But Shirley only smiled, a strange, luminous smile. "Oh, but they are, Mr. Moore. They are. They are a blind, maddened Sampson, pulling the temple down upon their own heads. She paused, her eyes searching his face. "Tell me, do you see nothing but the crime? Do you feel no flicker of pity for the desperation that must fuel such an act? Do you never lie awake at night and wonder if there is not a grain of justice in their grievance, however horribly expressed?"
The question hung in the air. Robert Moore stared at her, and for a moment, the hard mask of the man of business seemed to crack. A deep weariness, a profound trouble, shadowed his eyes. He looked from Shirley's challenging face to the quiet, still form of Caroline in the corner, as if just now remembering her presence.
"Caroline," he said, his tone softening almost imperceptibly. "You are here. I did not see you."
"I am always here, Robert," she replied, her voice so low it was barely audible. The simple words were a statement of fact, but they carried the weight of a long and lonely history.
His gaze lingered on her for a second, a flicker of some unreadable emotion in their depths, before he turned back to Shirley. "Pity, Miss Keeldar?" he said, his voice returning to its former harshness. "Pity is a luxury I cannot afford. Pity does not rebuild a broken frame. Pity does not pay the wages of the honest men who still wish to work. Pity does not stop a bullet. My brother was shot at in his own mill-yard last month. There is your 'grain of justice' for you."
He picked up his hat from the table where he had flung it. "I have said what I came to say. The soldiers are patrolling the Greenclose road. I am meeting with Captain Keir at the Red House in an hour. Be vigilant. Do not walk out alone." This last injunction seemed directed as much at Caroline as at Shirley. "Good-night."
Without another word, he turned and was gone. They heard his heavy, rapid footsteps in the hall, the opening and closing of the great front door, and then the sound of his horse, spurred again into a gallop, fading into the night.
The room he had left felt vast and empty. The air still seemed to vibrate with his restless, angry energy. The spell of the poetry, the peace of the evening, was not merely broken; it was shattered.
Shirley stood for a long moment, staring at the closed door. Then she let out a long breath and sank back into her chair.
"There," she said, her voice laced with a strange, tired admiration. "There goes a man. A hard man, a narrow man, a man of iron and fire, but a man nonetheless. He would not contend with Omnipotence, perhaps, for he does not believe in it. He contends with the next best thing: the world. Did you see his eyes, Caroline, when he spoke of his survival? He is a general in his own private war."
Caroline could not answer. Her throat was tight with unshed tears. The brief moment when he had spoken her name, when his eyes had met hers, had sent a pang of such exquisite pain through her that she could scarcely breathe. He had seen her, and yet he had not seen her. She was a fixture in his life, a cousin, a known quantity, as familiar and as unregarded as the rectory gate or the church spire. The vast, turbulent world of her love for him was a country on a map he never looked at.
"He is very unhappy," she said at last, the words a mere whisper.
Shirley looked at her friend, her own fiery energy softening into a deep, compassionate concern. "Yes," she said gently. "He is very unhappy. And you, my poor bird, have caught his winter's chill. He brings the storm with him wherever he goes, and leaves all in darkness when he departs."
She came and sat on the stool at Caroline's feet, taking her cold hands in her own warm ones. The volume of Scott had fallen to the floor, its pages open to the scene of battle. "He is one of my Titans, you see. A modern Titan, a Prometheus not of fire but of steam, chained to his mill as to a rock, and the vulture that gnaws his vitals is his own ledger-book, his own relentless ambition. And yet, he fights. I cannot help but admire the fight, even as I deplore the cause."
"He thinks we are foolish romantics," Caroline murmured, staring at the fallen book.
"Let him," Shirley retorted, a spark of her old fire returning. "Let him think us fools. He sees the world in black and white, in profit and loss. He does not see the colours of the sunset, nor hear the music in the wind. He does not understand a heart like yours, Caroline. And that, perhaps, is his greatest tragedy of all."
She squeezed Caroline's hands. "Come. The poetry is spoiled for tonight. The world has been too much with us, late and soon. Let us go to bed. Perhaps our dreams will be kinder than our waking hours."

The moon, not yet full, was rising, casting long, strange shadows from the trees and stone walls that lined the lane.

"Or perhaps," Shirley countered softly, "as if he were my brother. Is it not what we are supposed to do? Bear one another's burdens? Mr. Donne speaks of the 'flock,' but he sees only sheep to be sheared and penned. He does not see the individual soul, struggling and striving. He does not see the man. He sees only 'the poor,' a great, inconvenient mass to be managed and lectured at."
Caroline thought of Robert Moore. She thought of his mills, his struggles, his own view of 'the men' as a force to be controlled, a problem to be solved. Was he, in his own way, so different from Mr. Donne? Both saw the world through the lens of their own office, their own battles; one spiritual, one economic. Both, perhaps, failed to see the individual human heart.
"Robert sees them," she said aloud, almost to herself.
Shirley glanced at her, her profile clear and fine in the moonlight. "Robert Moore? What does he see, Cary?"
"He sees the hands," Caroline said, trying to give voice to the confused thoughts in her head. "He sees the men as 'hands' for his machines. He sees their potential for violence, their opposition to his frames, his progress. He calls them ignorant; he despises their resistance. And yet--I think he also sees their hardship. He does not condescend, like Mr. Donne. He fights them, as an equal enemy. He acknowledges their power, even as he seeks to break it. It is a terrible and a hard view, but it is not contempt. It is war."
"A fine distinction," Shirley murmured. "War instead of contempt. And in this war, where do the women and children stand? In the crossfire, I suppose. Like little Walter, who knows nothing of frames or curates, but only whether his father's arms are a safe place to be."
They walked on, the silence between them now filled with these new, harder thoughts. The soft, visionary mood of the early evening had been shattered, first by the tramp of soldiers, then by the cry of a child, and finally by the ugly little clash of social worlds. The idyll was over; the world, with all its complexities and conflicts, had intruded.
"He is very unhappy," Caroline said again, the words a sigh in the cool air, and this time she knew Shirley would understand she was not speaking of William Farren, nor of Mr. Donne, but of Robert.
"Yes," Shirley replied, her voice gentle. "He is one of our unhappy Titans, chained to his mill. And you, my poor Caroline, are chained to him. Your heart follows him into his battles, and suffers his wounds. Tonight, you saw me fight a very small skirmish, with words as my only weapons, against a very weak foe. Think of the war he is fighting, against desperate men, with his fortune and perhaps his life at stake. It is no wonder his brow is furrowed and his heart is closed."
"It is not closed to you," Caroline said, a faint, familiar ache of jealousy piercing through her weariness. "He speaks to you. He seeks your company."
"He seeks my money, Caroline," Shirley's reply was blunt, but not unkind. "Or rather, the use of it. He sees me as a potential ally, a capitalist with a fortune to invest. He speaks to me of trade, and machinery, and the London market. He does not speak to me of his heart. I doubt he even knows where to find it himself. He has locked it away, for fear it might interfere with business."
She stopped and turned to face her friend, her hands firm on Caroline's shoulders. "Do not mistake his commerce for confidence, my dear. The part of him that matters, the part that could love and be loved, is in a deeper sleep than any child in a church pew. And what will wake him? I do not know. Perhaps nothing can. Perhaps some men are made only for struggle, and find their only peace in the grave."
The starkness of the words hung between them. It was a bleak prophecy, a dismissal of hope. And yet, coming from Shirley, it felt not like a sentence, but like a sad, clear-eyed assessment of the truth. Caroline felt a tear escape and trace a cold path down her cheek. She did not brush it away. In the vast, quiet, moonlit darkness, surrounded by the sleeping fields and the distant, watchful moor, the single tear felt like a small, fitting tribute to a love that was as vast, and as silent, as the night itself. Shirley saw the glint of it, and her embrace became one not of argument, but of simple, human comfort. They stood thus for a long moment, two figures in the quiet lane, holding the line against the encroaching shadows.

It is in the church, and the church alone, that we find the prescribed remedy for the soul's ills.
